When I first started on Adderall mine were from Sandoz. I was on that for quite a few months before my pharmacy decided to mostly do Teva.

I much prefer the Sandoz generic, personally. Sandoz was great at cutting through my brain fog, allowing me to think more clearly. The first time I was prescribed the generic from Teva I noticed right away that it was much less effective at handling my ADHD symptoms than Sandoz. I had been taking 20mg twice a day of the Sandoz but I've since had to go up to 30mg twice a day with the Teva version and I still don't feel like I'm getting as much benefit from them. The Sandoz also seemed to last longer, whereas as I almost feel rather like an addict with the Teva because the benefits I do get just do not last.

I've thought about seeing if my doctor could specifically write for the Sandoz generic but have never gone through with it because, well, do I really want to give Walgreens another thing to fuck up on?

That being said, it's true that various generics affect people differently so maybe the Teva will be a perfect fit for you. If you have started taking the Teva already I'd be interested to know if you've noticed any difference. I've always been kinda curious as to if certain generics might work better depending on whether you're ADHD-PI/PH/C.

> So, next time she comes in yelling, tell her you're sorry about the messed up room, and show her something awesome you did instead.

Damn, every kid should know this advice...

Also, I empathise with your personal story about how you can still focus on SOME things. I actually study computer science at the moment at university, in high school I was getting D and E grades, but I did get a B in one subject, and at university I'm doing much better. I find programming easier to focus on because some problems can give instant gratification when you get something working. But if I'm doing something tedious, or couldn't find why there was a problem with the program, I found I couldn't keep going and got bored very easy. It's why I can program for 6 hours, but can't work on a math problem for 5 min before giving up.

I just started stims, and my focus has gone through the roof. Can't wait to see what I can achieve now.

Not at all! I absolutely get what you mean about hyper-focus. If I'm writing a paper, for example, and I get into that zone, I'll look up and realize it's five hours later and I've cranked out some serious work. That quality of ADD can be amazing when I can actually managed to get myself to hyperfocus on the stuff I need to work on.

It's tougher with this sort of thing, though, because it's very dry subject matter, and a lot of it is just "practice". There isn't a lot of creativity or problem-solving involved in the work, which is ironic, because there's a ton of creativity and problem-solving involved in actually doing this sort of thing professionally (server and network troubleshooting). It's why I want to do this for a living (right now I'm only doing it part-time). It's one of the few ways I can get myself to focus for a long period of time: if there's an unsolved issue, I can focus on that sucker and drill into it. I can get myself to not rest until I find the solution and *beat* it. If that makes sense.

i stopped by this sub reddit because i just went to the psychiatrist today due to problems with tiredness, memory, and motivation.  she broke me down in 30 minutes then prescribed me concerta.

your description of your morning sounds like mine.  i have a 15-20 minute conversation with myself about "do i really need a job?" and "being homeless wouldn't be so bad" and "i wish i could go to work unbrushed, unwashed in my mario pjs" until i finally convince myself the "pros" outweigh the "cons" and the biggest "pro" of all?  coffee.  i love coffee.  though lately even coffee isn't enough, hence the p-doc.

so my suggestion is to find/create some sort of reward.  sort of like what /u/603d3c94-c27d-4106-ae84-0612db0fa7ba said.  for me it's coffee, and "if i don't get my ass to work then i'm letting all these people down."  what it sounds like to me is you might not be medicated? or under medicated?  anxiety/shame/humiliation generate dopamine.  also, tell your professors.  tell them you're having trouble and ask them to hold you accountable.  if they aren't amenable get your school to help.

lastly, as /u/dcb0922e-cc4f-4122-a3d9-329ac9a24d64 said.  create a routine.  and don't think--just do.  buy 5 outfits keep them in a pile and don't think about it--just get dressed.  also, show up.  even if you're late.  show up and face the consequences.  times innumerable i've been late to places.  sometimes people are assholes, but i don't take it personally, because i know my limitations.

tl;dr create reward, create routine, ask for help you can't do it alone

All the time. May or may not be where I'm at right now, still trying to force myself to do something for this paper that I need to do entirely today...but I hardly even know what to do with it. I definitely know the feeling, getting overwhelmed because there's a lot of different tasks to do (or a lot of step to one task, or whatever) and then you can't focus on what part you need to do next (or even figure out what part that should be) because it all feels equally important or you try to start part of it but youre distracted thinking about how much else you'll need to do- and then you avoid making a decision by...going on reddit or something instead? And not accomplishing much at all? It happens to me way too much.

I definitely spent hours mostly just thinking about how much work I need to do this week and last week- instead of actually getting anywhere on the work. Wish I had advice to give on how to get out of that slump, but like I said, I'm still struggling with it too. With the large number of tasks I had I did end up writing out a painfully long list last week, and it did help some. Took a long time and was really the only "productive" thing i managed to do for the rest of that day, and it was based on when the absolute latest day I could start any of these tasks was. Not considering the amount of time theyd actually take (because i knew I should have started the essay I'm procrastinating now sooner, but it was due last and I didn't really have it in me to consider anything else at the time), and that obviously has some problems, but...that's all I've got so far.

Everyone also always recommends taking breaks but I have a hard time with that, because why should I take a break if I've just been procrastinating on my phone for 2 hours? Logically I know it could help to go do something else entirely but I guess I get guilty about it.

Just hoping someday I'll figure out a good way to work around that problem. And in the meantime, hoping I'll actually write this essay. Wishing you luck. Sorry for the rambling.

It might just be me but growing up with ADHD, you're probably lagging in focus and executive functioning. For example, I always felt that there way something missing in me. I couldn't pay attention to a conversation in a group setting. I would tune out completely beyond the 3 minute mark. I couldn't study unless I made myself feel immense pressure. All of this might, but not necessarily, lead to feeling of lack and feeling that you have something missing in you which l had for so many years. So when you feel weak, it is natural to have low expectations of yourself and to have a strong resistence to negative emotions. I taught myself how to detach myself from emotions and it really skyrocketed my productiving and my self image. The textbook has positive logical value but negative emotional value. So when you feel weak, you actually will avoid studying like the plague not because you cannot but because the anticipation of the negative feeling towards the book is too much for your fragile ego to handle.

When you feel weak, you will will have low standards for yourself so that your ego doesn't get bruized. When I raised my expectation of myself, it really did a lot for me.

Not saying your at fault or anything. I'm just giving you what was my problem and how I tried to fix it. Definitely, I still have trouble maintaining my ambition and focus towards my long term goals but I have made significant strides and finally feel a bit like a capable human being. Hope you figure out what works for you. I'm 27 btw if it matters to you.

I think it depends on what your coffee intake was before starting Adderall.  If you body is used to a certain level of caffeine intake I don't think it should be dangerous to mix the two.  But everybody is different so feel it out.  If you feel bad after mixing the two, don't mix them.

When I was taking generic adderall in smaller doses I had a couple of cups of coffee with it and felt fine, but I did have to cut down on my number of moka pots I brewed during the day.

To me it sounds like op isn't a big coffee drinker which could be why they're having such a marked response.

10mg is super low, 10mg was intended as a titration dose. The typical starting dose is 30mg which is to be increased at weekly intervals by 10mg until the therapeutic dosage is found. I'm currently on 40mg and I can tell it's too low. It wears off while Im still at work and I become distractible and unproductive. I'm hoping to get my doctor to increase the dose at the next visit but I feel like he doesn't really understand how to prescribe it properly so I'm looking to get a referral to a psychiatrist to get it sorted out. You should definitely try higher doses to properly assess whether it's right for you.

> Computer science. Something I'm still very passionate about,

Dude...  Seriously...

**ONE:**  Kiss of Death?  From a *high-school* English teacher?  heh.  Sorry...  Listen, you may like the guy...  You may admire teachers; maybe you've had some really good ones you respect.

My experience has been *much* different.  I have little to no respect for most of them.  Why?  Respect is earned, not given away.  Most of my "teachers" failed to earn mine.

I'm an adult, a grown man with a long and successful career in IT as a programmer.  If a high-school teacher were to confront me and attempt to insult me in any way, I would verbally eviscerate him.  Just sayin'.

And "All that would tell the school is that despite being smart, I don't know how to focus and apply myself."  No.  All that would tell anyone with a brain in their head is you didn't really bother to do the bullshit busywork they like to overload kids in High School with.  But clearly, you understand the material and can reason intelligently.

TL;DR; In my experience, I've found most teachers to be total fucking idiots.  I'd recommend not taking stuff they say too seriously.

**TWO:**  NO ONE in the IT industry gives a flying shit what sort of formal education I have.  Seriously.  (Don't believe me?  Ask others in programming subreddits.)  Come to think of it, only *once* did anyone in the IT industry ask or even care about college and my grades - it was someone from IBM, and it was for a shitty internship, a long, long time ago.

Since that time, every interview has always been about a few factors: What languages/skills do I have?  Can I prove it?  Am I passionate about programming and technology?  Am I an asshole?

That's pretty much it.  Get some marketable IT skills (it doesn't matter how.  Online tutorials, self-taught, college, adult edu classes, books...  whatever works for you.  ProTip: Head First books seem to work well for me with their somewhat unconventional format, but the problem with programming books is they can quickly become obsolete.  Online tutorials seem to work well.)

Be able to prove your skills.  Show them projects, source code, something you've done...

Practice interviewing and demonstrate passion about IT, learning new things and problem solving.

Don't be an asshole.  Try to be personable and helpful.  Don't be a pushover...  But just be a good guy that they'd want to hire.

**THREE:**  I'm not saying to *not* go to college.  College can be a great experience and not all teachers are idiots.  You've got to find your own path.  All I am saying is don't beat yourself up and don't despair.    "...failure should never lead to despair. Despair looks only to the past, in business, and in love."

**FOUR:**  My ACT and SAT scores were top-notch; my grades were shit.  I'm doing just fine.

Actually, even if I think about somehow changing my past - let's say I had a time machine and could give myself all A's.  I can't imagine my life being better than it is now.  My grades were that insignificant in the grand scheme of things.

You're going to get a lot of varied responses. All you can really do is talk to your doctor about it, experiment with it, and see what's best for *you*.

My personal anecdote though is that I am in the middle of quitting Wellbutrin. I have no confirmation yet, but do suspect it was lending to increased social anxiety. I didn't want to leave the house anymore. It was prescribed to help with ADHD symptoms, but didn't help enough. In addition to that, when I restarted Adderall, the adderall wasn't working like it used to pre-Wellbutrin. I still just wanted to sit around and do nothing.

I was taking the extended version of wellbutrin at 150mg. I don't think there's a lower dose, so my "stepping down" has been taking it every other day for a bit, then every two days, and then one final one after three days. My doctor didn't say I had to do this; he said I could just stop. I just know from prior experience that my body doesn't handle that as well as most people.

I *do* feel like my adderall has been working better for me as I'm nearing the final stages of quitting the wellbutrin, but its a bit early to say for sure. I expect it will take a bit longer still for the social anxiety to ease up (if the wellbutrin was the cause).

I know the feeling.

For the most part, I’m able to maintain my composure so even when I’m angry or upset, you wouldn’t know it. But if another person is angry and repeatedly provokes me, my defenses get activated and I can’t control myself. I either lash out and return their anger, or I try to hold it in and just find myself blinded with rage.

I meditate daily too, but that isn’t enough. I try to avoid these situations to begin, but sometimes they’re unavoidable, especially when it comes to people you care about who you spend a lot of time around. I understand that they’re probably on autopilot when their emotions take over, so the worst possible thing I can do is engage their ego by fighting back. Everybody thinks they’re right and if you approach any argument or disagreement from the position of “you’re wrong”, no matter how right you feel you are, you’re just making them more defensive. And the way I see it, if we assume that dealing with difficult people is an inevitability, then the only thing I can change is myself. I can’t always avoid the situation nor can I control my anger, so I figure the strategy I’ll use for my next argument will be to just respond by being really weird/silly because maybe that will snap them out of the trance. Anything to avoid taking the bait and jumping into an argument that will go nowhere, lol.

Just for both you and him to know -- there are reasons some of the stimulant meds made him feel like a zombie as a kid. Things like how it affects the emotional centers of the brain, as well as the overall balance of brain activity when kids are young. However, the dose of stimulants can absolutely be adjusted to prevent that side effect, and there are other non-stimulant options (like guanfacine)  that can broaden the range of symptoms that are treated so that a lower dose of stimulant works.

With meds, I feel more cheerful, playful, joyous, and happy, because I finally feel effective. It doesn't sound like he has as much emotional baggage from his diagnosis... it's just to note that taking the meds in no way compromised those feelings for me :) And if they did for him, the meds could be adjusted.

Not to push either of you towards meds -- just to let you know that they don't have to make you a robot zombie (that is a stereotype born from unfortunate conditions where psychiatrists didn't titrate the medication well for a child, or where families didn't communicate with the psychiatrist enough for titration to take place), and the things you love about him could persist after medication if that was something he wanted to try.

Edit to add: I also agree with everyone here -- that ability to see where it isn't malice, and to make it about behavior and not character is so fantastic. You're doing great, and he is luckier than you might even realize. That kind of understanding from someone without ADHD is really rare. Keep problem-solving, and don't be afraid to involve him. "This is important, can this be changed? Mind trying some approaches with me to see if something works?" Rewards also help so much more than punishment.

I don't really have time to write more, but you have such a solid foundation for making this work. Gives some of the rest of us some hope -- at least speaking for myself, it does. :)

It's not you, it's retail. Seriously. Retail fucking blows. Stores tend to understaff to save money and then call themselves 'fast paced' because they want one person to do the work of two, the hours are crap, store managers are (no offence to anyone) generally just sales assistants who stuck it out long enough to be promoted and aren't going anywhere with their lives and know this is as good as they'll get, so they power trip.

Seriously, it is probably one of the least ADHD friendly jobs out there, especially if you're inattentive ADHD (like I am). They expect robots, you're expected to put up with shitty customers and generally the work is monotonous (putting things out on shelves). You're also expected to do it 'their way' which takes away your ability to find ways to make things work for you.

Don't beat yourself up for being crap at retail.

In my family, my father has ADHD as well. Same thing. Could never hold down an entry level job but now he's a University professor and because he can largely make his own rules, he's thriving.

I have to sit at the very front of the class and take notes. Fidgeting has to be productive for me or else I will focus on the object of my fidgeting. So I just use different color pens and highlighters and take notes in multiple places like a notebook *and* a printout of a PowerPoint. I sometimes wiggle or bounce my feet around a bit.

Sitting in the front is the most important for me because it removes all potential visual distractions (does she know her tag is sticking out? Where did that backpack come from? Etc etc) between me and the lecture material.

I don't know if you have adhd, I couldn't tell you. But I'm just appreciative that healthcare in Australia is mostly free, I was only like $20 out of pocket to see a psychiatrist, and I got like 2 bottles of stimulants for like $14. It's sad that so many people aren't getting the examinations they need in order to see if there is something wrong with them, simply because they don't have the money.

In the meantime I'd try to do everything that you can do and see if it works. Like trying different techniques to discipline yourself or something, or plan out your day. I'm so impulsive that I'd make a plan and then completely ignore it. If it makes you feel any better, I got through university without meds and I have extreme trouble focusing and I'm extremely impulsive, I didn't have that hyper focus on what I studied because I didn't find it THAT interesting, but I found most the subjects interesting enough to get by.

Yup. I had an epiphany in January this year that depression and anxiety were not possibly not the problems but symptoms of the problem. This realization came as the result of therapy and introspection, so less of an epiphany and more the culmination of the work to be better. I'd hate to say that just the stimulant therapy itself has transformed my my mind but it's 90% of it. It has allowed my to think about things in a different way and has ultimately allowed me to find a path to happiness. All this time I'd been treating the symptoms, depression and anxiety, without addressing the underlying cause. Somehow I was able to create work around for the deficits and was fortunate enough to use my memory to offset the issues. My memory has been referred to by others as somewhat photographic and I believe this is why the underlying problem, ADHD, was masked. It's only recently that I've become aware that my thoughts and emotions are not the same thing. I understood what empathy is and could intellectually empathize but now I'm beginning to feel empathy as an emotional response. The stimulant therapy shuts my anxiety down almost like a switch, just gone. I've only had one minor several hours long depressive episode on the last several months and I know what it's about and unlearning long term notions isn't an overnight fix. I could go on and on but I think you get the idea.

I didn't have a drastic overnight change, but over time as I found the right medication and dosage for me, I did see improvement. And looking back on it, I realize how dramatic the difference is from when I wasn't medicated. It may take more than a few months for you to really spot the changes, but if your partner has noticed a positive change, then something is probably working.

Personally, I sometimes feel like I struggle with executive dysfunction even more than before I was medicated, but I honestly think it's because I learned more about it and became more self aware about the reasons behind all those difficulties I was having. So it can feel like I have so many executive function problems still, but I think part of it is that I can identify each one much more clearly.

Hi, I went off of Adderall about 10 years ago and have been medication free since.  It's not an easy transition, and took me years to become a highly - functional person without meds.

First, watch out for extreme mood swings when you stop.  I followed someone home and shouted them down in their driveway in the first week I went off meds, and I was coming off of just 5mg.  That is very unlike me, and who knows how you'll react.  You may want to step down gradually, but talk to your doc about it.

Next, try to maintain your current routines as best you can, but accept the fact that you won't be able to do everything the same way anymore.  You're giving up a major source of discipline and motivation, and your old habits will probably feel daunting and overwhelming for a while.  You'll wonder how you ever did them before.

So allow them to change to suit your new needs.  I recommend sticking with them as best you can so that you don't go off the deep end, and have some structure to fall back on when you don't know what to do with yourself.

And that's probably the hardest thing to cope with: inaction.  You'll have to look for your "tells" - the things you do when your ADD kicks in and you need to get back on track.  It's taken me years to recognize all the little ways I deviate from my tasks, and I still don't always catch them right away.

So I props this: make a list of your daily and weekly routines.  When you normally wake up, go to bed, brush your teeth etc.  Which day you do laundry, take out the trash, etc. etc.  Keep that list handy, so that when you come to on a Saturday evening and realize you just spent 10 hours playing video games, you can pick it up and do the thing on the list you would normally be doing.

And don't beat yourself up for the video games, just keep moving forward.

I hope that you're able to achieve what you're looking for.

I hyperfocused for the first time on a test last week and I agree with your assessment, it was pretty awesome feeling like I got it all together. When I left the exam room I checked the time and I was shocked because I thought I was in there for three hours but instead I had only been in there for one hour!!

Meanwhile today I’m struggling to string together a couple sentences and I’m just zoning out the entire time while trying to study for another test :(

I feel like my brain is a thunderstorm. I don't feel smarter than most people. But most people don't seem to pick up on everything I notice? Every distraction is fighting for equal attention of my brain, and I have to give it to all of them. Most people can just tune out distractions, automatically sorting them. But I manually have to pay attention to every small thing, classify what it is, and then go back to what I'm doing. I think it keeps me sharp. Also another pro is, I don't really get bored. When I go for a run or a long drive, that thunderstorm in my head is always thinking. Making me think of things that have happened, problems in my life, etc and I just think about them and how I should approach them. ADHD is a blessing and a curse though. I'm MUCH lazier than my friends because my brain does give me so much stimulation that I don't need to go outside my bubble to seek more.

I know. And if that happens, I would obviously discontinue use. However, my anxiety is a LOT better after starting on lexapro. ADHD is something that impregnates my day to day life, and just because it might increase my anxiety, it doesn't mean I shouldn't try it. Also, I will either only take it once or twice a week to complete the week long projects I do, or just take it on week days. I don't want a high dose, but I know it is a miraculous difference that I want, I need, to try.

I see music as a way to redirect my brains focus to something that is in front of me.

I absolutely love to have them in individual based work where I don’t need to listen to anyone. It still can wander but I feel like it is more controlled? I don’t know what the right word would be, but if I was to pick one, I’d say redirect focus. As if music reminded my brain to focus.

Doesn’t work much in social situation because I can be a chatter box so words from the music would just give me unnecessary ideas and words I might use.

And if I do find a song I like, like get hyped about it, I do tend to listen the shit out of it. With time I would begin to have it engraved to the back of my brain, know it word for word, involuntary. I don’t mind it at all, but then I find a new one and add that too a playlist.

I have a playlist with my favourite songs, or the ones that used to be my favourite. So I can listen to it or just play one particular. Depends what I feel like.

Although, I have found that having a specific playlist for individual things is helpful. Eg. Song for focus. Song for reading. Song for sleeping. Or a playlist. It seems to put me in this mindset of focus. That might help.

I hope I answered your question

Because when i take my meds, sure i can concentrate more, be more productive but i notice a change in my personality and behaviour. I tend to be more withdrawn, participate in conversations less, act differently than i would usually. Many of my friends have even noticed the difference and most of them dont even know i have ADHD, they just see the difference within 10 min of interaction. Medications used to treat ADHD fall in one of two categories: stimulants and non-stimulants. Stimulants are considered first-line pharmaceutical treatment for ADHD and you've tried two so far. It sounds like you're not getting good results with the medications you've tried so far so it might be reasonable to request a trial of something else. You might get better results with an extended release formulation of methylphenidate or mixed amphetamine without as many side effects. (You also wouldn't have to take this multiple times per day). I've also heard good things about vyvanse but this is a newer medication and can be very expensive if you're insurance won't cover it.

It's just important to realize that not all brains are the same; every medication used to treat ADHD won't be equally helpful for every person with ADHD. Work with your psychiatrist and be honest about your symptoms to find the medication and dose that works best for you. It's totally possible that you have some other things going on that might be complicating your ADHD and making you less responsive to medication (lots of ADHD patients have other issues like learning disorders, depression/anxiety, etc that make their ADHD more difficult to treat). You'll just have to keep trying until you figure out what's going to work for you.

I've definitely seen some improvement in my mood, focus, and motivation at work with stimulant medication. I feel calmer, more capable, more perceptive, and interested in what's going on around me. Before it would take a huge amount of effort to start any task and follow through with it but now I can just do what I need to do. Don't get me wrong, I can definitely still get distracted. It's not a miracle pill. But when I've got work to do I know I'll be able to get it done.

The best piece of advice I can offer is that you try not to think to much about your symptoms throughout the day. Don't allow yourself to hyperfocus on how the medication is/isn't helping you. Instead, take just a few minutes at the end of your day to reflect on your symptoms throughout the day. Maybe take a few notes that you can bring to your doctor so he can see how the medication is affecting you. This way it's not totally consuming every waking moment and further distracting you from work or school.

Besides the parent who spent all day in bed, I kinda gone through the same thing, with video game addiction and all. I am now 27yo, and it is still a struggle, to be honest, and I am saying that while I am having two jobs, as a neuroscientist and as a neuropsychologist. So yeah, CBT is something you should consider, because now I do work 40 hours a week at least, and it is still not good enough. While you are at 20/80, you think you will be satisfied when you reach a different number, but you don't. Even though you can rationally say to yourself: yeah, I am doing a great job, you still won't completely *feel* that way because of how you've developed yourself.

So please consider therapy, because if you feel you need to change, you need a proper tool. And just like you use a tool such as a saw to work on wood, you use a therapist to work on yourself. Choose someone that has not only experience with ADHD and CBT, but also someone that can go a little deeper (psychotherapy-like), because your problems are partly ADHD, partly the way your personality/personality structure developed. A good therapist can offer you things that you cannot offer yourself in this process, i.e. having a more unemotional/objective view of your situation, asking questions you did not think of, keeping your attention on the problem at hand, etc etc.

I have ADHD and my husband and all of our 3 children have been diagnosed with it recently as well.  We delayed meds for our oldest until 8. We mostly homeschooled until then in a low stress very laid back environment.  She started school recently and although the school is so different from a typical school and has a wonderful set-up for children with ADHD we decided that it was important academically for her to be more calm and able to focus better in class. We also believe that school before 8 school is mostly for fun and socialization. We eat fairly cleanly because it is important to us. Although we are food dye free I honestly notice a bigger different when we avoid all processed foods especially sugar. Food is fuel for the body and mind and the best fuel gives you the best performance.

We have the children on a fairly set routine. They really thrive when they know what to expect. Every week I write out a new calendar and every day at breakfast we talk to the kids about what to expect.  Right now our schedule is very difficult because each of our children goes to a different school.

We are working on teaching the children about emotions. I myself as part of my ADHD am hyper-sensitive. Each of the children is different but all show signs of being hyper-sensitive. Each of us find dealing with emotions difficult.

Some things that have helped us with our routine. Our home is very small and all three kids share 1 room. Each time we do laundry we hang a complete outfit on a hanger and we only keep less than 10 outfits in the closet in their room at a time. It's very easy for them to get dressed and ready by themselves.  We also limit the number of toys out in there room. Too many toys and they pull them all out and are completely unable to put them away. I also make sure that they get adequate screen time each day because the ability to focus on just one thing like a game can be a nice stress relief. They do more chores than the average child their age because it's going to take starting early for them to build healthy habits for life. We are just starting the time of year where it is cool enough for the kids to start spending more time outside doing physical activity. When the kids get really frustrated we have them go outside and run. We always play classical music in the car.

When the kids get really frustrated or overwhelmed we hit the pause button on whatever we are doing and we stop and explain anything.  It took us a while to learn that being a couple minutes late is absolutely worth it when we have completely calm children.

This reminded me of something else I've seen, which is that it's also a problem with the time until the consequences happen. If there are no consequences or they are far off an abstract, then the motivation to do the thing tends not to be there.

I run into this a lot myself with things like personal art projects and sometimes even work projects. Since there's no consequence for me not doing the thing, my ability to focus on and do it fizzles very quickly.

Ok, you're doing what you can on that end. And you're trying to get in with specialists. I'm not trying to be an armchair psychologist here, but it sounds like you're dealing with more than your fair share of anxiety, due to your situation and naturally through ADHD (isn't that a great side effect?). And honestly, I think you're doing the best you can do right now. You're making schedules, you've developed habits to deal with your symptoms, you've contacted professionals... that's a lot of healthy coping. Right now is the hardest part, the time between being pushed overboard and the first appointment.

If you can't hold yourself accountable, then work while someone else is present. Do what works for you, and try not to beat yourself up for failure. You're doing the best you can do right now while dealing with this, and that might not be enough for other people, but try to have it be enough for yourself for the moment. And, in my personal opinion just throwing it out there, maybe look into a therapist as well as your ADHD doctor so you can work through some of your anxiety and work on other healthy practices.

I got through high school because I had a strong support system. I was in a program for students with learning disabilities, I am dyslexic as well, and in retrospective the things they had me do were more designed to help me with adhd then dyslexia. I had an hour long study hall all 4 years where I had to meet with a counselor and tell them what I was working on and what I had to finish. I got extended time for tests. I was not allowed to become to disorganized, I had days in the middle of every semester where all I was allowed to do was reorganize myself. All that helped and allowed me to develop really very good coping mechanisms.

The first 2 years of college kicked my ass and I almost dropped out. I had to learn how to cope on my own and spent the better part of my college career struggling with work. I finally went into a psych and was diagnosed with adhd. I've been on adderal for 5 days now and honestly it's like my brain just calmed down.

I wish I had been diagnosed sooner but my mom is convinced it's a made up disorder. That stimulant medicines are awful and that you just need to work harder or different. So Ya I got diagnosed at 22 but have been struggling unmedicated my whole life.

Honestly I thought a lot of what I was dealing with was normal and I just wasn't as smart as my peers. I am really angry I was not diagnosed in high school because I have lost a lot of chances because of it.

Get to my mom's place and . . . nobody is there. I had forgotten the shower was at a restaurant closer to my sister's house, 50 minutes away! I leave in such a rush that, half-way to the restaurant, I realize I've left all the shower games, the gifts, and get well soup at my mom's place.

That's when I lose my s***.

I thought I was doing so well. By the time I got to the shower, I was so frustrated with myself I couldn't walk into the room without bursting into tears. Not only did I show up an hour late empty handed but I stole all the attention from my sister by looking like a complete moron with a bunch of maternal figures closing in to make sure I was okay.

I wanted to die. I had taken on too much with the two work schedules and I had no idea how stressed I was until overlooking that one tiny detail sent all my efforts straight to hell. Then the dam broke . . . in front of a bunch of friends and relatives.
